title: One Night on URANUS Lasts 42 Years 😴
description:
Your night lasts eight hours. On Uranus, at the pole, one night lasts about 42 years. The whole planet is lying on its side, so as it rolls around the Sun, your pole turns away for half the trip. One trip takes 84 years: half of that in the dark. It has been night at Uranus's south pole since 2007, and the next sunrise there is in 2049. Morning, Grandpa.
Day or night: which 42 years would you take?

The science: Uranus's axis is tipped about 98 degrees (97.77°, NASA), so it spins on its side and rolls around the Sun like a ball. It takes 84 Earth years to go round once, so each pole gets roughly 42 years of sunlight and then roughly 42 years of darkness. The last equinox was on 7 December 2007: the Sun set on the south pole, and the north pole saw the Sun for the first time in 42 years. The next equinox, and the south pole's next sunrise, is in 2049. (The 42-year night is at the poles; NASA describes a dark winter of about 21 years for half the planet.) Bonus: a day on Uranus is only about 17 hours, and its cloud tops hold hydrogen sulfide, the gas that makes rotten eggs smell. (The planet's face and its pillow are jokes.)
